text.p: Pennsylvania's legislature early Tuesday approved a plan to deregulate the state's electricity market, sending the bill now to the governor, who earlier said he would sign it, a spokesman at the governor's office said.
"The bill was approved at 1015 (EST) last night (Monday) by the Senate and by the House about 0200 EST this morning," said Steve Miskin, a spokesman for Governor Tom Ridge.

Ridge, in a prepared statement, said "This legislation will mean lower electric bills for working Pennsylvania families, more jobs for working Pennsylvanians, and more choices for Pennsylvania consumers...I will gladly sign this bill into law."
Pennsylvania becomes the fourth U.S. state to enact legislation deregulating its electricity industry, following California, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island.
Neighboring New Jersey is expected to unveil the second phase of its study on electric utility deregulation by the end of the year.

The legislation seeks to give one third of the state's consumers an opportunity to choose their electricity supplier by the end of 1998, expanding retail competition to include all consumers by January, 2001.

Under the new law, the state's Public Utilities Commission can order utilities to conduct pilot competitive retail programs from April 1, 1997, tapping for each program five percent of a utility's peak load for at least a year.
The response from the main investor-owned utilities operating in the state was generally positive.

"GPU Energy certainly agrees with lawmakers that competition will be more effective than regulation at lowering prices and stimulating economic development," said Dennis Baldassari, president of GPU Energy, a unit of GPU Inc.

Other key utilities operating in Pennsylvania include Pennsylvania Power & Light Co, units of PECO Energy Co, DQE Inc, Ohio Edison Co, Orange and Rockland Utilities Inc, UGI Corp, and Allegheny Power System Inc.
Consumer groups have also lent support to deregulation.
"We supported the bill. It was a good compromise that will hopefully bring lower rates," said Irwin Popowsky at Pennsylvania's Consumer Advocate Office.

The sticky problem of how utiltiies recover stranded investments as they move from a regulated to an open market is covered by issuing transition bonds, with any savings realized from this scheme put toward further rate reductions.
According to the law, municipal and rural power cooperatives are not required to participate in retail competition unless they decide to market power outside their traditional service territories.
